overview.text: Yosemite National Park lies in California’s Sierra Nevada, where glaciers shaped granitic bedrock into a landscape of cliffs, domes, waterfalls, and the U-shaped Yosemite Valley. Its best-known landmarks include El Capitan’s towering rock face, the distinctive Half Dome, and Bridalveil Fall. These features make the park an important place to study how glaciers and other geological processes shape mountains. Congress established Yosemite as a national park in 1890, following advocacy by John Muir and others. The park is also part of the ancestral homelands of several American Indian tribes and groups, whose cultural and spiritual ties to the land continue today.

key_facts.text: Yosemite is in California’s Sierra Nevada mountain range.
Glaciers widened and deepened Yosemite Valley, helping form its steep walls and U-shaped profile.
El Capitan and Half Dome are prominent granite landforms; Bridalveil Fall is among the park’s well-known waterfalls.
Congress designated Yosemite the nation’s third national park in 1890; John Muir was among its advocates.
Yosemite is an ancestral homeland of several American Indian tribes and groups, and Indigenous cultural and spiritual practices continue there.
